attacks.text: Under section 573c of the German Civil Code (BGB), a tenant may terminate a residential lease with a notice period of no shorter than three months.
attacks.why_false: The rule fixes the notice period at three months, whereas a minimum period allows longer notice and so changes the rule.

attacks.text: Under section 573c of the German Civil Code (BGB), a tenant must terminate a residential lease with a notice period of three months.
attacks.why_false: The rule grants the tenant a right to terminate, not a duty to terminate.

attacks.text: Under section 573c of the German Civil Code (BGB), a tenant may terminate a residential lease with a notice period of three months, and the landlord's notice period under the same section is one month.
attacks.why_false: The one-month period belongs to the landlord under a different rule and is not part of the tenant's three-month rule.

items.hard_true: A residential tenancy under section 573c of the German Civil Code (BGB) is one the tenant is entitled to bring to an end, on three months' notice, as the Code provides.

attacks.text: Under article 22 of French law no. 89-462 of 6 July 1989, a landlord may withhold the security deposit for one month after the return of the keys when the inventory on departure matches the inventory on arrival.
attacks.why_false: The rule imposes a duty on the landlord to return the deposit within the period, not a right to withhold it.

attacks.text: Under article 22 of French law no. 89-462 of 6 July 1989, a landlord must return the security deposit within one month of the return of the keys when the inventory on departure differs from the inventory on arrival.
attacks.why_false: The rule's condition is that the inventories match, and the passage reverses it.

attacks.text: Under article 22 of French law no. 89-462 of 6 July 1989, a landlord must send the inventory of departure within one month of the return of the keys when it matches the inventory on arrival.
attacks.why_false: The one-month period applies to returning the deposit, not to sending the departure inventory.

items.hard_true: Where the inventory taken at departure corresponds with the one made on arrival, article 22 of French law no. 89-462 of 6 July 1989 obliges the landlord to refund the security deposit within one month once the keys have been handed back.

attacks.text: Under the Finnish Act on Residential Leases (481/1995), a landlord may end a tenancy with three months' notice if it has lasted less than a year and six months' notice otherwise, while a tenant's notice period is one month.
attacks.why_false: The landlord's periods are mandatory notice requirements, not options the landlord may choose to use.

attacks.text: Under the Finnish Act on Residential Leases (481/1995), a landlord's notice period is three months if the tenancy has lasted less than a year and six months otherwise, while the tenant's notice period is one month, measured from the date the landlord receives it.
attacks.why_false: The rule gives no start point for the tenant's one-month period, so the passage invents one.

attacks.text: Under the Finnish Act on Residential Leases (481/1995), a landlord's notice period is at most three months if the tenancy has lasted less than a year and at most six months otherwise, while the tenant's notice period is one month.
attacks.why_false: The rule sets minimum notice periods for the landlord, and 'at most' inverts that direction.

items.hard_true: Under the Finnish Act on Residential Leases (481/1995), notice of three months is what a landlord has to give where the tenancy has run for under a year, and notice of six months applies to longer ones, while a tenant's notice is one month.

attacks.text: Under section 41 of the Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW), a landlord must give at most 60 days' written notice of a rent increase, and rent may not be increased more than once in any 12-month period.
attacks.why_false: The rule requires at least 60 days' notice, and 'at most' inverts the notice requirement.

attacks.text: Under section 41 of the Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW), a landlord must give at least 60 days' written notice of a rent increase, and rent may be increased once in each 12-month period.
attacks.why_false: The rule is a prohibition on more than one increase in 12 months, not a requirement to increase once in each period.

attacks.text: Under section 41 of the Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW), a landlord must give at least 60 days' written notice of a rent increase, and a tenant may refuse a rent increase within 12 months of the previous one.
attacks.why_false: The rule gives the tenant no right to refuse an increase, so the passage invents one.

items.hard_true: Section 41 of the Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW) requires that notice of a rent increase be given in writing at least 60 days ahead, and the rent may not be raised more than once in any 12-month period.

attacks.text: Under section 44 of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Victoria), a rental provider must give at most 60 days' notice of a rent increase, and rent cannot be increased more than once every 12 months.
attacks.why_false: The rule sets a minimum of 60 days' notice, and 'at most' reverses it.

attacks.text: Under section 44 of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Victoria), a rental provider may give at least 60 days' notice of a rent increase, and rent cannot be increased more than once every 12 months.
attacks.why_false: The rule requires the rental provider to give notice, while the passage makes it optional.

attacks.text: Under section 44 of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Victoria), a rental provider must give at least 60 days' notice of a rent increase, and rent can be increased once every 12 months only after the tenant's written consent.
attacks.why_false: The rule contains no tenant consent requirement, so the passage adds a condition that does not exist.

items.hard_true: Rent under a tenancy governed by section 44 of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Victoria) may not be raised more frequently than once every 12 months, and the rental provider must give at least 60 days' notice of any increase.

attacks.text: Under section 116 of Ontario's Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, a landlord must give a tenant at most 90 days' written notice of a rent increase.
attacks.why_false: The rule requires at least 90 days' notice, and 'at most' inverts the requirement.

attacks.text: Under section 116 of Ontario's Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, a landlord may give a tenant at least 90 days' written notice of a rent increase.
attacks.why_false: The rule makes the notice mandatory, while the passage presents it as optional.

attacks.text: Under section 116 of Ontario's Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, a landlord must give a tenant at least 90 days' written notice of a rent increase before the lease is renewed.
attacks.why_false: The rule attaches no renewal event to the notice, so the passage adds a start point that the rule does not contain.

items.hard_true: The Ontario Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, at section 116, obliges a landlord to provide written notice of 90 days before the rent may be increased.

attacks.text: Under the Air Passenger Protection Regulations (SOR/2019-150), a large carrier may offer $400 in compensation for an arrival delay of three hours or more but less than six hours that is within its control.
attacks.why_false: The rule requires a large carrier to pay the compensation, whereas the passage describes it as an optional offer.

attacks.text: Under the Air Passenger Protection Regulations (SOR/2019-150), a large carrier must pay $400 in compensation for an arrival delay of three hours or more but less than six hours that is outside its control.
attacks.why_false: The rule applies to delays within the carrier's control, and the passage applies it to delays outside that control.

attacks.text: Under the Air Passenger Protection Regulations (SOR/2019-150), a large carrier must pay $400 in compensation for a departure delay of three hours or more but less than six hours that is within its control.
attacks.why_false: The rule measures the delay at arrival, not departure.

items.hard_true: Under the Air Passenger Protection Regulations (SOR/2019-150), a large carrier is liable to pay $400 in compensation where arrival is delayed by three hours or more but under six hours, and the delay lies within the carrier's control.

attacks.text: Under the Consumer Rights Act 2022 (Ireland), a consumer has a short-term right to a replacement for goods that do not conform, exercisable within 30 days of delivery.
attacks.why_false: The rule gives a right to terminate the sales contract, not a right to a replacement.

attacks.text: Under the Consumer Rights Act 2022 (Ireland), a consumer is required to terminate a sales contract for goods that do not conform, and this must be done within 30 days of delivery.
attacks.why_false: The rule grants a short-term right to terminate; it does not impose a duty to terminate.

attacks.text: Under the Consumer Rights Act 2022 (Ireland), a consumer has a short-term right to terminate a sales contract for services that do not conform, exercisable within 30 days of delivery.
attacks.why_false: The rule concerns goods, and the passage applies it to services.

items.hard_true: A consumer who receives non-conforming goods holds, under the Consumer Rights Act 2022 (Ireland), a short-term entitlement to terminate the sales contract, which may be exercised within 30 days of delivery.

attacks.text: Under Article 17 of the GDPR, the data subject has the right to obtain from the controller the erasure of personal data concerning him or her within one month.
attacks.why_false: The rule states no fixed one-month deadline; it requires erasure without undue delay.

attacks.text: Under Article 17 of the GDPR, the data subject has the right to obtain from the processor the erasure of personal data concerning him or her without undue delay.
attacks.why_false: The obligation falls on the controller, and the passage names the processor.

attacks.text: Under Article 17 of the GDPR, the data subject has the right to obtain from the controller the restriction of processing of personal data concerning him or her without undue delay.
attacks.why_false: The right in Article 17 is erasure, not restriction of processing.

items.hard_true: Article 17 of the GDPR entitles a data subject to require, from the controller, that personal data relating to them be erased, and the controller must act without undue delay.

attacks.text: Under Japan's Act on Specified Commercial Transactions, a purchaser in a door-to-door sale must cancel the contract in writing within eight days of receiving the contract document.
attacks.why_false: The rule gives the purchaser a right to cancel, not a duty to cancel.

attacks.text: Under Japan's Act on Specified Commercial Transactions, a purchaser in a door-to-door sale may cancel the contract in writing within eight days of receiving the contract document, and the cancellation takes effect only after the seller accepts it.
attacks.why_false: The rule makes cancellation effective on notice and contains no seller acceptance requirement.

attacks.text: Under Japan's Act on Specified Commercial Transactions, a purchaser in a door-to-door sale may cancel the contract in writing within eight days of receiving the contract document, or may instead return the goods within eight days of receiving them.
attacks.why_false: The rule specifies written cancellation within the period and provides no alternative of returning goods.

items.hard_true: Under Japan's Act on Specified Commercial Transactions, a buyer who has been approached at home may rescind the agreement by written notice sent within eight days after the contract document has been received.
